title: Pictures That Stick
tagline: A Roman handbook, a man with a goat on his head, and twelve ways to make any picture impossible to forget.
card: Why the strange and the loud are remembered and the ordinary is not, and a checklist for building pictures that stick.
goal: you will learn what makes a mental picture memorable, use a twelve-point checklist (SMASHIN' SCOPE) to build one, and turn a plain word into a picture you could not forget.

left_off.q: Name the three stages of memory.
S. remembered long lists without writing them down. What did he do with each item?
left_off.a: He turned it into a vivid picture, often with colour, and put it along a street he knew.

left_off.q: Why is a chunk easier to hold than ten separate letters?
left_off.a: Working memory holds only a few units. A chunk counts as one unit even when it contains several letters or digits.

story.heading: The man with the goat on his head

text: Imagine a morning in Rome, two thousand years ago. You cross the Forum on your way to a lesson. You pass a hundred things: stalls of olives, a woman arguing about the price of cloth, a boy with a basket, the same stone steps you climb every day. At the end of the day someone asks you what you saw. You can hardly say. It was all ordinary, and ordinary things slip straight through the mind.

Now imagine that halfway across the square a man comes towards you wearing a bright red wig, leading an elephant by a string, with a live goat balanced on his head. The goat is chewing a letter. You would remember him for years. You might not even need to try.

check.q: Why do you forget most of what you pass in the Forum?
check.a: Because it is ordinary. Ordinary things do not stand out, so the mind does not keep them.

parts.talk: What is the strangest thing you have ever seen in the street? How long have you remembered it?

text: The Roman author who made this point in a handbook on public speaking, written around 85 BC, is unknown. For centuries people thought it was Cicero. The handbook is called Rhetorica ad Herennium, and it says something very close to the Forum story. We remember little things, ordinary things, everyday things, it says, because nothing about them surprises us. But anything shocking, ugly, beautiful, funny, huge or unbelievable stays with us a long time.

So the advice for anyone who wants to remember is make the picture unusual. Do not hold a polite, realistic picture in your mind. Give it colour, make it move, make it louder and bigger than life, make it a little silly or a little shocking. The handbook adds that the pictures should be active: people doing things, not still lifes.

check.q: What does the Roman handbook say about ordinary things?
check.a: We forget them because they do not surprise us. Striking, strange, beautiful, funny or huge things are the ones we keep.

parts.talk: Why do you think a funny or shocking picture is easier to remember than a calm one?

text: People have been rediscovering this ever since. Modern memory trainers have turned the advice into a checklist you can use to build a picture on purpose. One popular version is a twelve-letter word, SMASHIN' SCOPE, and you will learn it in the next tab. Each letter is a way to make a picture richer: add a sense, add movement, add a joke, add a number.

There is a catch, and it is a good one. The picture has to be yours. A picture borrowed from someone else, however wild, does not hold as well as one you made, because making it is the work that fixes it in the mind. This room is where you start making them.

check.q: Why should you make your own pictures?
check.a: Making the picture is the work that fixes it in memory, so your own picture holds better than someone else's.

parts.talk: Describe, in two sentences, a picture you could use to remember the word Monday.

image.cap: a room of pictures nobody would forget

words.m: so unusual or strong that you notice it at once. a striking image
very strange and surprising. a bizarre picture
to make something bigger or stronger than it really is. Exaggerate the size.
normal, with nothing special about it. an ordinary morning

source: The handbook is the Rhetorica ad Herennium (c. 85 BC), Book III. Our own paraphrase.
method_heading: Twelve ways to make a picture stick

method.x: A good memory picture is not a photograph. It is a small film with something happening in it, and it breaks the rules of real life.

head: Letter
Idea
What to do
rows: Mix the senses. Taste a colour, hear a shape, smell the scene.
Make it move: fly, spin, crash, run.
Connect it to something you already know well.
Add strong feeling: touch, taste, delight or disgust.
Break the rules of the real world.
Count it: three hundred ducks, one giant.
Use a symbol: a crown for a king, a heart for love.
Make it bright, or the wrong colour.
Put things in a clear order or pattern, or stack them in an odd one.
Pleasant pictures are easier to return to than horrid ones.
Make it enormous or tiny. Overdo everything.

one tool is good.
three or more

method.title: Building one picture
lines: An orange as big as a car.
It rolls down the High Street, bouncing off lamp-posts.
You smell the citrus, hear the crunch, feel the spray of juice on your face.
People run away screaming, holding tiny umbrellas.
method.pic: A car-sized neon orange rolls down the street, crunching lamp-posts and spraying juice, while people run away under tiny umbrellas.

method.x: When the word is not a thing

You can picture an orange. You cannot picture justice or Brazil or lecture. For those you substitute: find something you can see that sounds like the word, or means something close to it, and picture that. Brazil sounds like bra; Russia sounds like rushing; lecture can be a person talking at a lectern. You will do a great deal of this in the rooms to come.

items.x: A word you can see, or a substitute for it.

items.h: Add three tools from the checklist.
items.x: Size, colour, sound, humour, a number.

items.h: See it for a few seconds.
items.x: Close your eyes. It is a picture only if you can see it.

method.x: Describe the orange picture aloud, and add one more tool from the list that is not in the example.

try.title: Which tool is this?
try.prompt: Match each detail to the letter of SMASHIN' SCOPE it uses best.
pairs: The pen is ten feet tall.
The pen is spinning and spraying ink.
The pen smells of strawberries and sounds like a trumpet.

try.title: Build it together
try.prompt: Make a picture for BICYCLE using at least three tools. Think: how big? What colour? What is it doing? What can you hear and feel? Write your picture in a sentence or two.
try.model: A bicycle as tall as a house, bright pink, is pedalling itself down a staircase, ringing its bell like a fire engine. You can feel the whole building shaking, and a hundred pigeons burst out of the windows.
checks: It is bigger, odder or louder than real life.
It uses at least one sense besides sight.
It uses at least three tools from the checklist.

try.title: Your turn: PENCIL
try.prompt: Make a picture for PENCIL. Use at least three tools. Write it down.
try.model: A pencil the size of a tree trunk, glowing gold, is writing your name on the sky with a scraping sound that makes your teeth ache. Rubber dust falls like snow.
checks: It uses at least three tools.

try.title: Your turn: HAMMER
try.prompt: Make a picture for HAMMER. This time try to use Sensuality (strong feeling), Number and Humour.
try.model: Seven tiny hammers are tickling your feet, and every time one taps you laugh so hard you cannot stand. They are bright green and ring like bells.

items.s: A picture is easier to remember if it ___ (it is not still).
When a word is hard to picture, we ___ it with something that sounds like it.
To remember "Brazil", you might picture a giant ___.

try.q: Which picture is the best memory picture for the word LEMON?
opts: A lemon the size of a bus, bright yellow, sliding down the road and squirting juice at every car.
A lemon next to an apple.
try.why: It uses size, colour, movement and a bit of humour. The first and third are real-life, calm pictures, which the mind lets go.

try.title: Describe it aloud
try.prompt: Pick one of the pictures you made and describe it aloud in sixty seconds. Add as many senses as you can while you speak.

cards: Mix and use the senses: taste, sound, smell, touch as well as sight.
Make the picture move. A still picture fades.
Connect it to something you already know well.
Add strong feeling: delight, disgust, touch.
Funny pictures are easy to return to.
Break the rules of real life.
Use a symbol that carries meaning.
Pleasant pictures are easier to return to.

quiz.q: How many items are in the SMASHIN' SCOPE checklist?
quiz.why: Twelve letters: S, M, A, S, H, I, N, S, C, O, P, E.

quiz.q: What should you do with a word like "justice" that you cannot picture?
opts: Substitute a picture that sounds like it or stands for it
quiz.why: Substitution: for example a judge with scales, or a giant dice, that stands for it.

quiz.q: Why does making the picture yourself work better than borrowing one?
opts: Because making it is part of what fixes it in memory
Because borrowed pictures are always dull
It does not make any difference
quiz.why: The effort of creating the picture is what builds the memory.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest set of tools for a picture of CLOCK?
opts: A small clock on a wall
A huge, red clock melting down a wall and ringing like a siren
quiz.why: Size, colour, movement and sound: four tools.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: eight words in ninety seconds
challenge.intro: Make a vivid picture for each word, using at least three tools. Study, then type what you remember.
challenge.study: Do not repeat the words. Build one wild picture for each, a few seconds each.

look_back.q: What are the three stages of memory?

look_back.a: A group of things you treat as one unit, like FBI or a year.
Right after learning, then it slows. So the first review matters most.

look_back.q: Why was S.'s memory sometimes a problem for him?
look_back.a: He could not forget; old pictures piled up and got in the way.

can_do: explain why strange, vivid pictures are easier to remember than ordinary ones.
use at least three tools from SMASHIN' SCOPE to build a picture.
turn a word I cannot picture into a picture by substituting a sound-alike.
reflect: Pick a word from today you found hard to picture. What did you substitute, and why did that work?
